$schema_note: AUTHORED, and deliberately small. One entry per platted block claimed from the 665-roof programme's schedule (data/reconstruction/1835_665_roof_programme.json, derived by tools/reconcile_665.py). Expanded into ordinary one-file-per-structure records by tools/generate_block_infill.py, which tools/check.sh re-derives. This file authors NO coordinates: every metre comes from the committed lot polygons in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and every dimension from the family bands in 1835_family_archetype_crosswalk.json. What is authored here is which family stands on which lot, whether it fronts the street or the alley, and how far back it stands.
why_the_schedule_is_copied_here: The schedule is DERIVED from what stands, so a block's family mix is erased the moment the block is built — it becomes at_capacity with no mix at all. A generator reading the live schedule would therefore write ten records on its first run and none on its second, and the re-derivation gate would fail on the commit that shipped it. `drawn_from_schedule` and `families` are the claim a parcel made against the schedule at the moment it claimed it, frozen so the expansion stays reproducible. tools/generate_block_infill.py checks the slots against them; tools/reconcile_665.py re-derives the schedule from the result.

placement_rule.principal: One principal roof per lot, standing back from its own street frontage, its facade to the street and its walls parallel to the block face. The setback is a period typology and not a measurement of this lot.
placement_rule.ancillary: A yard building off the block alley, behind a principal roof on the same lot, facing the alley.
placement_rule.open_lots: Alternating open lots are intentional and are what the phase-one parcel already assumes. A block at capacity is a claim about 1835 that the evidence does not support; the schedule's capacity is a ceiling.
placement_rule.what_is_invented: All of it. Which family stands where, which lot is left open, the setbacks and the lateral offsets are inventions bounded by the programme, not readings of a source. No lot is numbered: this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet, and the side lot lines and the alley are conjectural even where the block face is not.
placement_rule.density_standard: THE CORE DENSITY STANDARD (T-0079), which raises the two rules above and is what T-0028's successors inherit. Until this parcel a block's ceiling was one principal roof per platted lot, and a party-line run carried exactly one roof per lot it was dealt — so a row was exactly as dense as the lot grid, and "a row is denser than the lot grid" was a sentence with no arithmetic behind it. Two things retire that. FIRST, the dataset already exceeds the ceiling: five of the twelve core blocks the plat module reaches stand at 11, 12, 13, 14 and 14 roofs against a ceiling of 10, put there by the reviewed phase-one parcel and by the documented record, so the rule was only ever refusing the NEXT roof. SECOND, it counted in the conjectural unit: the side lot lines are conjectural — every record here says so in its own position note — while the block FACE is committed geometry derived from the street centrelines. So the ceiling is now a frontage count of THREE units per lot, measured at the worst case in tools/reconcile_665.py: the smallest lot on the committed grid carries 23.56 m of frontage, the plat module keeps 1.5 m clear of a side line at each end of a run, and the eighteen committed party-line units average 6.072 m wide, so (23.56 - 3.00) / 6.072 = 3.39 units fit on the meanest lot in the town and the fourth does not. THE THREE CLAUSES A PARCEL WORKING TO THIS STANDARD APPLIES: a commercial frontage tightens toward party-line spacing rather than standing a cottage in the middle of each lot; an improved lot carries its outbuildings; and a corner lot BUILDS TO THE CORNER, which is what the `corner: west` anchor added by T-0079 is for — an east-anchored run packs back toward the corner and stops wherever its roofs run out, so the corner was the one piece of frontage a row could never reach. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: capacity is still a ceiling and not a target, a principal roof still needs a free lot to stand on, a block still keeps a lot open, and the 665-roof total does not move — the roofs a raised ceiling admits come out of the district balance `south_plat_beyond_committed_control`, which fell from 175 to 120 when the standard was raised.
placement_rule.frontage_fabric: THE FRONTAGE-FABRIC RULE (T-0022, legacy K29), and it settles a question two liberties left open. L99 and L100 both recorded the worry that the 665-roof programme “has no notion of what a street was for” and “will keep dealing cabins to commercial frontage”, and K29 proposed the remedy that follows from believing it — a schedule term weighting the meanest dwelling families off the business front. MEASURED, THE WORRY IS BACKWARDS AND THE REMEDY IS REFUSED. The evidence is three-fold and none of it is taste. (i) The documented record already puts log buildings on the principal-street line and they are TRADE buildings: hogan_store (log, a store, on South Water), philo_carpenter_log_shop (log, a drug shop, on Lake), madore_beaubien_house (log, dwelling and store, on South Water), mansion_house (log, a tavern, on Lake); one street back, james_kinzie_house is a documented log RESIDENCE on Lake. (ii) The only picture of this row — “South Water Street in 1834”, image 11 of the owner's brief of 2026-08-18, the same plate this file already cites for the party-line treatment — draws it as “roughly ten one-storey LOG AND FRAME buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river”. This project accepted the half of that sentence about shape and ignored the half about fabric. (iii) The owner's ruling of 2026-08-27 on PR #371's fork, option (b): a business-front lot may carry a documented store at the street and an anonymous dwelling behind it, so the business front is not a district a dwelling is kept out of. THE RULE, THEREFORE: a block face on a principal street of the committed street hierarchy (data/streets/1835.json, traffic=principal) is dealt its party-line row WITHOUT ranking the dwelling families by tier. A log dwelling may take a unit of that row and takes the west end of it where the block was dealt one, so the row reads log and frame as the plate draws it. What this REPLACES is the arrangement the South Water recipes state in their own prose — “the two best dwellings the schedule deals take its two free lots … and the two meanest take Lake” — which was a preference, was in no source, and had left 15 invented buildings on South Water's line with not one log among them. WHAT DOES NOT CHANGE: the schedule itself. No family total moves, no roof is added or removed, and no record changes family, footprint or form — five log dwellings and the five frame dwellings they change places with are the same ten records they already were. tools/measure_frontage_fabric.py holds the result and tools/check.sh runs it.
placement_rule.end_rule: THE END RULE, AND ITS CRITERION IS THE WALK (T-0023, ROADMAP K31). The rule decides which of the roofs a block was dealt stands where along its frontage, and the claim it makes is unchanged from T-A8: the better roof stands nearer the Dearborn Street drawbridge, the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835. NO SOURCE SAYS THIS. It is an invention of this programme, it always was, and every record that applies it says so in its own position note. WHAT CHANGES IS HOW THE DISTANCE IS MEASURED: from 2026-08-27 it is the distance WALKED along the committed street centrelines from the roof's own frontage to the bridge's south abutment — not T-A11's straight line to it. Run tools/measure_end_rule.py and quote it; do not re-argue it. WHY, IN THREE MEASURED PARTS. FIRST, the straight line measures how far away the BLOCK is and not where the roof stands on it: its worst step between two neighbouring party-line units falls from 6.06 m on the blocks a kilometre out to 0.52 m at blk_randolph_clark, so it goes blind as a block approaches the bridge — weakest exactly where the bridge matters most, because the bridge's bearing swings round toward the face and the criterion only ever sees the sine of the angle between them. SECOND, it is below the floor on TWELVE OF THE TOWN'S THIRTY-SIX PLATTED BLOCK FACES, the back face of blk_south_water_clark — the block T-A11 wrote the rule on — among them. The floor is not invented for the occasion: it is the 3.50 m range of setbacks THIS FILE deals its own 48 principal slots (4.0 m to 7.5 m) and grades, three keys above, `a period typology and not a measurement of this lot`. A setback moves a roof along the face's outward normal, which is broadly the axis the end rule grades along, so a criterion separating two neighbouring roofs by less than that range is grading the placement's own declared invention. THIRD, the walk is scale-free: a metre of frontage is a metre of walk on every face of every block, so its step is the party-line unit's own 6.072 m on all thirty-six faces and it cannot be exhausted by where the bridge happens to bear. AND IT MOVES NOTHING THAT STANDS, WHICH IS WHY IT COULD BE TAKEN AT ALL: the two criteria name the same nearest lot on 36 of 36 platted block faces. K31 warned that the successor must not be chosen on a block where it agrees with the old rule; the answer is that they agree EVERYWHERE, so no block could ever have discriminated between them, and the choice was never about which roof goes where. Nothing already built is re-graded, L102 onward stand verbatim, and every arrangement note written before this date is left as it was. THE RULE ALSO GAINS A FLOOR, because the exhaustion went four blocks unnoticed. Where the criterion's step between two neighbouring roofs falls at or below that same declared setback range, the parcel RECORDS THE WITHIN-FACE ORDER AS ARBITRARY instead of claiming a grading. Under the walk no committed face is in that position, so the clause binds nothing today; it exists so the next exhaustion is caught by the command rather than by a fifth block. WHAT THE RULE IS NOW ASKED TO DO, and it is not what it was built for: until T-0079 a block carried one principal roof per platted lot, so the end rule ordered LOTS, about 24.6 m apart. The core density standard retired that ceiling and a party-line run now stands three units on ONE lot, about 6 m apart — so since T-0079 the rule has been ranking the front doors of what the plat calls a single property, and no parcel said so. Under the straight line that step was 0.52 m to 3.53 m on the row and the rule had nothing left to deal; under the walk it is the unit's own width.
placement_rule.non_dwelling_placement: THE FACE RULE RANKS DWELLINGS, AND A NON-DWELLING IS PLACED BY ITS FUNCTION (T-0024, legacy K32). The face rule as committed at T-A13 and T-A14 orders DWELLINGS: the best the schedule deals a block take its better street, the meanest take the back one. blk_randolph_clark was the first block parcel ever dealt a STORE and the rule said nothing about one, so T-A15 EXTENDED the ranking to cover it — commerce above the better dwelling, on the reasoning that a store-residence's claim on the better frontage is functional rather than social, 'the only one of the six roofs whose purpose requires that a stranger can find it'. That extension was an invention about 1835 commerce made by an agent and was opened as K32 for the next block dealt a commercial family to follow or refute, because the schedule still holds C1…C4, F1…F4, H3, T1 and W1…W5 for blocks not yet built and a warehouse's answer is plainly the opposite of a store's. SETTLED ON THE SECOND OF THE THREE READINGS THE ROADMAP OFFERED: the face rule ranks dwellings only, and a non-dwelling is placed by its own function. Reading 1 was to keep the ranking and reading 3 was to refuse the question and leave it to each parcel's arrangement note; reading 2 is taken because it is the only one of the three that can be READ OFF THE COMMITTED RECORD rather than argued. WHAT THE RECORD SAYS, over the 48 documented buildings this project's own reconciliation credits a non-dwelling family, by the traffic class data/streets/1835.json authors for the street each stands nearest: STORES 15 records, 10 principal, 5 ordinary, 0 light; WAREHOUSES 9, all nine principal; WORKSHOPS 7, two principal, five ordinary, 0 light; LODGING 8, three, four and one; INSTITUTIONS 9, one, four and four — and the institutional families are refused to a block parcel by name (L93), so no frontage rule reaches them. NOT ONE documented store, warehouse or workshop stands on a light street: a zero across 31 buildings, on the three letters a block parcel may actually be dealt. Lodging's one is the Steamboat Hotel, 287 m from the State Street centreline, which does not front it. THE TWO CLAUSES. (1) A non-dwelling takes the block's BETTER face by the committed street hierarchy, and a store, warehouse or workshop may never take a light one — an invented one would be the first in Chicago. (2) A COMMERCIAL roof stands ON the street line rather than back at a dwelling's typology setback: every documented store standing on a platted street stands on its line, and thirteen of the fifteen are inside the measured street-line band, the two outside it being Robert Kinzie's store at Wolf Point and the Miller house, both off the platted grid. The line is the closest one the plat module's own margin allows, which is the same line the party-line runs already stand on across this town. WHAT MOVED: one roof. blk_randolph_clark's C2 store-residence came forward from 4.5 m to that line, out of the row of house setbacks it had been standing in. NOTHING ELSE MOVED, and that is the finding rather than a convenience — on the one block the question has been asked, reading 1 and reading 2 put the store on the same face, so the ranking could be refused without re-arguing a block that already stands. tools/generate_block_infill.py refuses a slot that breaks either clause and tools/measure_face_rule.py holds the reading the clauses are taken from; tools/check.sh runs both.

blocks.arrangement_note: The block stood empty. Seven of its eight lots take a principal roof and the eighth is left open. The two larger houses take Randolph, which is the through street of the pair, and the rougher dwellings take Washington: that is a typology of frontage value, argued from the street hierarchy the plat module measures, and it is not evidence about this block. The three yard buildings serve the lots they stand behind — a stable behind the merchant's house because that is the household with a horse, a privy behind the other Randolph house, a woodshed behind the log dwelling on Washington. Each of those is a reason for the roof, not evidence for it.

open_lot.why: A south-tier interior lot, left open so the block does not read as a completed terrace. Which lot is arbitrary within the block; that one is open at all is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy.

deferred.why: The schedule deals this block one civic or public-service roof and the parcel refuses it rather than massing it. I3 resolves through the fort_structure placeholder, whose entire vocabulary of building kinds is garrison words — quarters, barracks, blockhouse, magazine, store, guard, sutler, artillery — and none of them names the adapted office or the engine house the crosswalk says this family spans. Massing an anonymous town civic building through that archetype would not merely guess at a function; it would stand a garrison building in the middle of the platted town, three quarters of a kilometre from the fort. The crosswalk already states the precondition on its own entry: the six-roof aggregate spans unlike functions and they must reconcile to named public records before construction is selected. A dwelling nobody named is the ordinary case in this town; a public building nobody named is a claim that an institution existed and left no record, and the two are not the same kind of anonymity.

blocks.arrangement_note: The easternmost block the plat module covers on the Randolph tier, bounded by Randolph, State, Washington and Dearborn, and empty in this dataset before this parcel. The schedule dealt it ten roofs and no house or commercial family at all — five dwellings across the rough end of the range, four yard buildings and the civic roof this parcel defers. Five principal roofs on eight lots leaves three lots open. What is argued here and not found: the three better-built dwellings (the deep-plan and two-room cottages and the one-room cottage) take the Randolph face because Randolph is the through street of the pair in the module's own street hierarchy, which is the same frontage-value typology the Randolph and Wells block recorded, and the log cabin and the plank shanty take Washington. The four yard buildings each stand behind a principal roof on its own lot, because a rear yard belongs to a lot and a lot belongs to a house. The barn or carriage shed takes the eastern end lot, where the block backs onto ground the plat module does not reach and the town gives out; that is a typology of where a town keeps a large animal shelter, not evidence about this block.

open_lots.why: A south-tier interior lot, left open on the same alternating-vacancy assumption as lot 4.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first West Division block this module reaches, bounded by Randolph, Canal, Washington and Clinton, and the first block off the reconciled schedule that was NOT empty when the parcel arrived. Three anonymous roofs from the pre-plat West approaches parcel already stand inside it — recon_1835_west_018, _019 and _021, placed from typed coordinates months before the plat module existed, so no record of theirs names a lot. The generator derives which lots they hold from their own committed footprints rather than being told, and refuses a principal roof on any of them; the schedule's headroom of seven is the block's headroom and never a licence to stand a second house on an occupied lot. RE-ARGUED ON THE TRANSPOSED GRID (T-1734), and `frontage_argued_on` above is the field that says so rather than prose anybody has to find. The owner ruled on 2026-09-23 (T-1479, option a) that the West Division's own module may cut a block printing no lot figure of its own, and this block — plat block 45, whose ten numerals the sheet prints inside it — is now cut that way: two columns of five backing onto a north-south alley, ten lots where there were eight, every one of them fronting Clinton or Canal and not one of them fronting Randolph or Washington. The deal below was argued face by face against Randolph and Washington when it was claimed, and the transpose removes both of those faces, so the argument had to be MADE AGAIN and not relabelled — which is why this block waited while T-1733 transposed its twin `blk_lake_clinton` at once, that one carrying no deal to re-argue. WHAT THE RE-ARGUMENT KEPT, AND WHY IT COULD. The old argument ranked the block's two faces off the committed street hierarchy (data/streets/1835.json) and gave the two better dwellings the better street: Randolph is `ordinary` and Washington is `light`, so the deep-plan and two-room cottages took Randolph and the log dwelling and the one-room cottage took Washington. The same hierarchy ranks the new pair the same way — Canal is `ordinary`, Clinton is `light` — so the RULE survives the transpose and the faces change under it: the deep-plan (D5) and two-room (D4) cottages take Canal, the one-room cottage (D3) and the older log cabin (D1) take Clinton. That the ranking held is a fact about the hierarchy and not a confirmation of the typology. Had Clinton outranked Canal all four roofs would have crossed the alley, and this sentence would have been written the other way about. WHAT CHANGED BECAUSE THE GEOGRAPHY DID. The old note sent the barn or carriage shed to “the western end lot, where the block backs onto ground beyond Clinton that has no committed street control and the town gives out”. On the transposed grid there is no western end lot — the two columns run north and south, and the alley runs down between them — and the lot that answers that description is the Clinton column's southern end, lot index 4, the block's south-west corner. The barn stands there, in the yard of the log cabin, which is the same reasoning applied to the arrangement the sheet gives instead of the one the town scheme gave. The stable keeps the deep-plan cottage's yard and the privy the one-room cottage's, which is the pairing the first deal already had; only the lots they are in moved. WITHIN EACH FACE the order is the end rule's (placement_rule.end_rule): the better roof stands nearer the Dearborn Street drawbridge, and on a north-south face that is the northern end, so D5 stands north of D4 on Canal and D3 north of D1 on Clinton. Three lots are left open rather than one, because the transpose gave this block two lots more than the deal it carries was sized against and a parcel does not raise a roof it was never dealt in order to fill new ground. Which three is arbitrary within what the standing roofs leave, and each entry says so. None of it is evidence about this block. Every metre below comes from the committed lot polygons; the families, the lots, the setbacks and the lateral offsets are inventions bounded by the programme.

open_lots.why: The Clinton column's one remaining free lot, between the standing west_019 roof at the column's north end and the one-room cottage dealt below it, left open. The programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy puts the gap between two occupied lots rather than filling the column, and the schedule's capacity of ten is a ceiling and not a target.

open_lots_taken_since.why: named open by this deal for the programme's alternating vacancy on the Canal face; raised by T-1761 against hh_bennett_h_c's standing D3 request. The gap that reason asks for has moved to the Clinton face rather than been given up — see the second deal's arrangement note, which argues the move instead of dropping this sentence.

named open by this deal because nothing had been dealt to it when the transpose cut the block to ten lots; raised by T-1761 against hh_adams_james's standing D7 request, which is a household asking by name and not the re-cut adding a roof.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first South Division block of the Randolph row, bounded by Randolph, Franklin, Washington and Market, and the first block off the schedule whose standing roofs were put there by THIS project's own inferred-household layer rather than by a pre-plat coordinate parcel. inf_sawyer_dwelling_a and _b hold lots 4 and 6 — the two sawyer households of the occupation census, placed from typed coordinates before the plat module existed — so the block arrives with its Randolph face half built and both remaining free lots on that face. That is what decides the arrangement: the through street fills first, and the vacancy the programme requires has nowhere to fall but the Washington face. What is argued here and not found: the deep-plan and the one-and-a-half-storey cottages take the two free Randolph lots, because Randolph is the through street of the pair in the module's own street hierarchy and carries the west-side crossing — the same frontage-value typology the three Randolph-tier blocks before this one recorded. The two-room and the one-room cottages take Washington, the back street. Lots 1 and 5 are left open in alternation with them, and lot 1 is the one named first because it is the Washington-and-Market corner: Market is the river edge of the South Division here, and the corner nearest the wharves and the lumber ground is the least attractive residential lot on the block. The barn or carriage shed takes lot 7, the Franklin end of the quiet street and the furthest point on the block from the Randolph-and-Market bridge approach — the same where-a-town-keeps-a-large-animal-shelter typology the two blocks before this one applied at their own quiet ends, tested here against a third geometry rather than repeated. The stable, the woodshed and the privy stand behind the cottages on their own lots. None of it is evidence about this block, and no lot is numbered.

open_lots.why: A Washington-tier interior lot, left open in alternation with the two this parcel builds on, which is the pattern the phase-one parcel already assumes and the only face of this block with room left to express it: the Randolph face arrived with two of its four lots already carrying a roof and the schedule's headroom fills the other two.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first block off the South Water row, bounded by South Water, Wells, Lake and Franklin, and the first block this lane has taken on the town's BUSINESS front rather than one street back from it. It arrives with three roofs standing and none of them anonymous: the Temple Building holds lot 0 at the South Water and Franklin corner, the Exchange Coffee House holds lot 7 at the Lake and Wells corner, and J. H. Kinzie's forwarding store laps the north edge of lot 2 without taking any of its buildable part (T-A7 measured that at 9.7 m², all of it in the 1.5 m margin strip). What is argued here and not found: South Water is the valuable frontage of the pair — it is the river street, it carries every documented commercial roof near this block, and the module's own street hierarchy ranks it above Lake — so the three deepest dwellings the schedule deals take its three free lots, and the two meanest take Lake, the back street. Within each face the better roof stands nearer Wells, because Wells is the town-centre end of this block and Franklin the lumber-and-wharf end: the deep-plan cottage takes lot 6, the two-room lot 4 and the one-room lot 2, and on Lake the log cabin takes lot 5 against the shanty on lot 3. The one-room cottage is also the smallest of the three principal roofs the South Water face gets, which is the arrangement that leaves Kinzie's lap the most room — but the lap did NOT constrain the block, and saying so is the point of measuring it: lot 2's roof stands 7.3 m from that store against a 3 m separation gate, and every other roof this parcel places is further from its own nearest neighbour than that. The half-metre of extra setback on lot 2 was authored with the lap in view and turned out not to be needed. A reader should not have to re-measure to find out whether the standing commercial roofs squeezed this block; they did not. The stable takes the yard of lot 3 — the quiet street's far end once the Lake and Franklin corner is left open — which is the same where-a-town-keeps-a-large-animal-shelter typology the three blocks before this one applied at their own quiet ends, tested here against a fourth geometry rather than repeated. The privy stands behind the two-room cottage on lot 4. None of it is evidence about this block, and no lot is numbered. THE LOG UNIT JOINS THE ROW, AND THE FACE RULE THAT KEPT IT OUT IS RETIRED (T-0022, legacy K29). This block's arrangement above sent the meanest dwelling the schedule dealt it to the back street on the reasoning that South Water is the business front. Measured, that was backwards: it left 15 invented buildings on South Water's line with NOT ONE of them log, against a documented record for the same line carrying Hogan's log store, and against the only picture of this row — “South Water Street in 1834”, the plate this recipe already cites for the party-line treatment itself — which draws it as “roughly ten one-storey LOG AND FRAME buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river”. The half of that sentence about shape was taken and the half about fabric was not. So the log dwelling and the frame cottage below CHANGE PLACES. The D1 log dwelling comes off Lake lot 5 and takes the west end of the South Water run, sharing its party wall with the D4 cottage it now abuts; the D3 one-room cottage takes the Lake lot the cabin held, at the same 5.5 m setback and the same 1.5 m offset the cabin stood at. On the row the cabin's nearest neighbour that is not its own party wall is 5.81 m away, and off it the cottage stands 19.90 m from the Exchange Coffee House. NOTHING ELSE MOVES AND NOTHING IS ADDED: both records keep the id, family, footprint and every form value they already had — the slots keep their positions in the list precisely so the ids do not shift — the block's roof count, family mix and open lot are the ones the schedule dealt, and no household is re-homed. The schedule was never the fault; the arrangement was. tools/measure_frontage_fabric.py holds the result. THE OWNER CHANGED THE DENSITY STANDARD ON 2026-08-27, AND THIS BLOCK IS ONE OF THE FOUR IT REACHES. Everything above was written while the street's documented stores stood OUT IN THE PLATTED ROADWAY, because their setback had been read off a 2026 kerb line instead of off this project's own plat. T-0198 and T-0199 put all eleven of them back on the committed frontage, and on the plat they SEAT — on lots this parcel's frontage run had already been dealt. Nothing overlapped: every one of the eleven was checked against every committed footprint in the town and the worst overlap is zero. What refused the repair was a RULE, one principal roof to a lot, and it was refusing the town's own business front. The fork went to the owner because it decides what a South Water lot IS rather than where one building stands, and he ruled that A PLATTED BUSINESS-FRONT LOT MAY CARRY A DOCUMENTED STORE AT THE STREET AND AN ANONYMOUS DWELLING BEHIND IT — the geometry already permits it, and the alternative would have paid eight roofs and two households for a rule the corrected data had itself called into question. THIS PARCEL LOST NOTHING: every roof it was dealt still stands, on the lot the recipe named, and no household moved. The clause is bounded and its three tests are written into tools/plat_occupancy.py. ON THIS BLOCK, RE-MEASURED: Kinzie's forwarding store no longer laps lot 2 at all — reconciled with the plat under T-0198 it also moved 24.39 m WEST, in its own note's stated direction, and now seats on lot 0 beside the Temple Building, which is why this parcel's lot 2 roof stands 41.37 m from it rather than the 7.3 m measured above. The 9.7 m² margin-strip lap reported above was true of the old placement and is kept here as the reading it was, not as a description of the ground today. THE FRONTAGE DECLARATION WAS MEASURED AND NOT CORRECTED (T-0449, 2026-09-12): see `frontage.runs` for the reach of the run against the lots this entry names, and tools/measure_frontage_declaration.py for the town-wide reading — fourteen frontage entries, three over-declared, all three on this row.

open_lots.why: The Lake-and-Franklin corner, left open. Franklin is the lumber-and-wharf end of this block and Lake is its back street, so the corner where the two meet is the least attractive residential lot the block has — the same tier reasoning the Randolph and Market parcel applied to its own back-street corner. Which lot within the tier is arbitrary; that a block on the business front is not a completed terrace one street back is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.

frontage.why: T-0078, and the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18 with it: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." The reference he supplied for this reach — "South Water Street in 1834", the south bank of the Main Branch — shows a CONTINUOUS WORKING ROW: one-storey log and frame buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river, the street between them and the grassy bank, two-storey frame stores anchoring its east end. This block's anonymous roofs stood seven metres back from that frontage, a full lot apart, each nudged off the line by its own lateral offset and — because the placement rule takes its bearing from the way into the lot — facing the block's interior rather than the river. That is the shape of a distribution across a block, not of a street. They now stand ON the frontage: the line, its bearing and the end they pack back from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and this recipe authors no coordinate for any of them. The 1.5 m setback is not a measurement of this frontage — it is the closest line the plat module's own lot margin allows, adopted so the street wall is one wall. NO ROOF IS ADDED: the run carries exactly the roofs the schedule dealt this block's frontage lots, with every id, family and dimension the one it already had. What the view drives is the treatment — a row on its line, facing the water — never a coordinate, and the side lot lines the row crosses between its own units were conjectural in every record this generator has ever written. blocks.arrangement_note: The fourth block of the South Water row, bounded by South Water, Dearborn, Lake and Clark, and the first on which the row's “better roof nearer the town-centre end” rule can be pointed at something instead of asserted. The three parcels before this one named a direction; this block's east end is Dearborn Street, and the Dearborn Street drawbridge — the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835, a committed structure record whose south abutment stands at the foot of Dearborn on South Water — is 35.6 m from lot 6's frontage, 55.5 m from lot 4's, 78.1 m from lot 2's and 101.7 m from lot 0's. The same gradient runs along the back street, from 126.3 m at lot 7 to 158.2 m at lot 1. Nothing in that is evidence that a better house stood nearer the bridge; what it gives the arrangement is a stated, re-derivable criterion in place of a compass direction. Lots 0, 6 and 7 arrive taken — Harmon & Loomis's store, John Bates Jr.'s auction room and the first Tremont House — all three seated by tools/plat_occupancy.py rather than authored here, so the schedule's five free lots are 2 and 4 on South Water and 1, 3 and 5 on Lake, and this parcel builds on four of them. The face rule is T-A8's, carried one block east: South Water is the business front, so the two best dwellings the schedule deals take its two free lots — the deep-plan cottage on lot 4 and the two-room cottage on lot 2 — and the two meanest take Lake, the one-room cottage on lot 5 and the log cabin on lot 3, each of them the better of its pair nearer the Dearborn end. THE FACE RULE MEETS ITS FIRST COUNTER-EXAMPLE HERE AND THE PARCEL RECORDS IT RATHER THAN ARGUING IT AWAY: the largest documented footprint on this block stands on the BACK street. The first Tremont House covers 139.3 m² at the Lake and Dearborn corner against 92.9 m² for the auction room, 92.9 m² for Harmon & Loomis's store and 46.5 m² for Pruyne & Kimball's drug store. A hotel choosing that corner is evidence about 1835 and the face rule is not; the rule is kept because it is a typology for where anonymous dwellings of different tiers go, not a claim that Lake Street was worth less. THE MEASUREMENT THIS BLOCK OWES ITS READER IS ON LOT 2, and it is the fourth instance of T-A7's lap case and the first that costs a lot nothing at all: Pruyne & Kimball's drug store laps lot 2 by 4.66 m² of its 46.5 m², and 0.00 m² of that lap falls inside the lot's buildable inset — the whole of it lies in the 1.5 m margin strip. Two of the store's four corners sit 0.70 m and 0.65 m inside the platted lot line and the other two stand 5.4 m out in the roadway, a 5.55 m intrusion into the South Water corridor. Against the 22.1 m² inside the inset on the block one west, Kinzie's 9.7 m² and recon_1835_west_018's 11.9 m², the case now has four measured points. THE WEST OFFSET THAT ANSWERED THE LAST BLOCK'S LAP WAS MEASURED HERE AND REFUSED, which is the more useful half of it: on lot 2 an offset of 1.5 m buys 0.03 m of clearance and 3.0 m buys 0.33 m while costing 1.26 m of lot-line margin, where half a metre of extra setback buys 0.50 m on its own. Church's store stood deep in its lot, so sliding along the frontage moved a building away from it; this drug store stands in the roadway, so only standing further back from the street helps. The cottage is set back 7.5 m and clears the store by 6.83 m against a 3 m separation gate, the closest approach anywhere in this parcel; the remaining lateral offsets are jitter and are called jitter. Lot 1, the Lake and Clark corner, is left open. The privy takes the yard of lot 4 behind the deep-plan cottage, at the alley end and 24.53 m from the auction room, which is the only documented roof on this block standing anywhere near the alley. None of it is evidence about this block, and no lot is numbered. THE LOG UNIT JOINS THE ROW, AND THE FACE RULE THAT KEPT IT OUT IS RETIRED (T-0022, legacy K29). This block's arrangement above sent the meanest dwelling the schedule dealt it to the back street on the reasoning that South Water is the business front. Measured, that was backwards: it left 15 invented buildings on South Water's line with NOT ONE of them log, against a documented record for the same line carrying Hogan's log store, and against the only picture of this row — “South Water Street in 1834”, the plate this recipe already cites for the party-line treatment itself — which draws it as “roughly ten one-storey LOG AND FRAME buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river”. The half of that sentence about shape was taken and the half about fabric was not. So the log dwelling and the frame cottage below CHANGE PLACES. The D1 log dwelling comes off Lake lot 3 and takes the west end of the South Water run beside the D5 deep-plan cottage; the D4 two-room cottage takes the Lake lot the cabin held at the cabin's own 6.0 m setback and −2.0 m offset. The cabin stands 13.65 m from Pruyne and Kimball's drug store, which stands proud of the line in front of lot 2 — further off it than the cottage it replaced was, because the run packs west and the cabin is the narrower of the two. NOTHING ELSE MOVES AND NOTHING IS ADDED: both records keep the id, family, footprint and every form value they already had — the slots keep their positions in the list precisely so the ids do not shift — the block's roof count, family mix and open lot are the ones the schedule dealt, and no household is re-homed. THE OWNER CHANGED THE DENSITY STANDARD ON 2026-08-27, AND THIS BLOCK IS ONE OF THE FOUR IT REACHES. Everything above was written while the street's documented stores stood OUT IN THE PLATTED ROADWAY, because their setback had been read off a 2026 kerb line instead of off this project's own plat. T-0198 and T-0199 put all eleven of them back on the committed frontage, and on the plat they SEAT — on lots this parcel's frontage run had already been dealt. Nothing overlapped: every one of the eleven was checked against every committed footprint in the town and the worst overlap is zero. What refused the repair was a RULE, one principal roof to a lot, and it was refusing the town's own business front. The fork went to the owner because it decides what a South Water lot IS rather than where one building stands, and he ruled that A PLATTED BUSINESS-FRONT LOT MAY CARRY A DOCUMENTED STORE AT THE STREET AND AN ANONYMOUS DWELLING BEHIND IT — the geometry already permits it, and the alternative would have paid eight roofs and two households for a rule the corrected data had itself called into question. THIS PARCEL LOST NOTHING: every roof it was dealt still stands, on the lot the recipe named, and no household moved. open_lots.why: The Lake-and-Clark corner, left open, on the same tier reasoning the three blocks of this row before it applied to their own back-street corners: Lake is this block's back street and Clark the end that runs back west toward the lumber yards and the wharves. What is new is that the tier can be measured on this block rather than only named — lot 1's frontage is 158.2 m from the foot of the Dearborn Street drawbridge, the farthest of the eight lots from the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835, where lot 6 at the other corner is 35.6 m from it. That a block on the business front is not a completed terrace one street back is the programme's own assumption of alternating vacancy, and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target; which lot within the tier is still a choice, now a stated one.

frontage.why: T-0078, and the owner's standing ruling of 2026-08-18 with it: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." The reference he supplied for this reach — "South Water Street in 1834", the south bank of the Main Branch — shows a CONTINUOUS WORKING ROW: one-storey log and frame buildings shoulder to shoulder facing the river, the street between them and the grassy bank, two-storey frame stores anchoring its east end. This block's anonymous roofs stood seven metres back from that frontage, a full lot apart, each nudged off the line by its own lateral offset and — because the placement rule takes its bearing from the way into the lot — facing the block's interior rather than the river. That is the shape of a distribution across a block, not of a street. They now stand ON the frontage: the line, its bearing and the end they pack back from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and this recipe authors no coordinate for any of them. The 1.5 m setback is not a measurement of this frontage — it is the closest line the plat module's own lot margin allows, adopted so the street wall is one wall. frontage.runs: One run of two — this block was dealt only two frontage roofs, because Harmon and Loomis's store holds lot 0 and Madore Beaubien's house lot 6 — packed west from the east end of lots 2-4. redealt_2.why: THE ROOF COUNT DOES NOT MOVE AND ONE FAMILY DOES, and what moves it is a source about this lot rather than a rule about this block. G. Spring's For-Sale notice ran six times in the Chicago Democrat between 1834-06-18 and 1834-11-19 and four printings carry it whole: "LOT No. 7, in block No. 16, one lot east of Haddock's Tavern, on Lake street ... There is on said lot a large Dwelling-House and fine well". T-0423 seated that address on the roof whose footprint centroid falls inside the lot, which is the plat lot 7 this recipe builds as its own lot index 5 on the Lake face, and it declined to touch the fabric under it. So the card carried the notice's own word LARGE over a 5.36 x 6.38 m one-room frame cottage - the smallest dwelling family the schedule deals - and the town's answer to "what stood on lot 7 of block 16" contradicted the only source that speaks about that lot. THE SLOT IS RE-DEALT TO H1, the lowest rung that answers the notice's own two words. The crosswalk labels D6 and every D family below it a COTTAGE and D7 a SMALL two-storey house; H1 is 'Larger one-and-a-half-story house', the first family the crosswalk itself calls larger and calls a house, and 24x30-28x38 ft against the D3 band's 16x20-18x24. Taking the lowest rung that answers the adjective is the restraint: the notice says large and says nothing about storeys, paint, trade or wealth, so nothing above H1 may be read out of it. NO TOTAL MOVES. The 665-roof programme apportions H1's eighteen roofs to the districts and not to any block - 'a per-unit family mix is an apportionment of that district's remainder, not a claim about any block' - and the south district's remainder held eight unbuilt H1 before this run and seven after it, with the displaced D3 going back the other way, thirteen to fourteen. The block still builds six roofs, five principal and one ancillary, against the same headroom of six, on the same lots, at the same 5.5 m setback and -2.0 m lateral offset the cottage stood at. This is the town's FIRST H1: the family was dealt eighteen roofs in July 1835 and instantiated none, and the first one lands where a documented notice says a large dwelling-house stood. WHAT IS STILL INVENTED IS EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS AND THE GRADE DOES NOT MOVE. That any building stood on this ground, that this count-unit is that house, and every dimension of it are conjectural exactly as they were: 'lot 7' is a conjectural line bearing a documented number, the numbering was read off block 18 and counted, and the seating stays at the bottom tier where L216 put it. What changes is only that the invention is now bounded by the source instead of contradicting it. Recorded in docs/LIBERTIES.md and ruled in docs/LOT-ADDRESS.md.

open_lots.why: Lot 1 is the one lot on this block that nothing stands on, and since T-0827 that is not a choice any more. The block's lots moved 2.9 m west with `market`, which was re-fitted off the plat's own 400 ft module instead of off the modern junction on N Wacker Drive it had been hung from; the packer's dwelling did not move with them. It had lapped lot 3 from lot 1 by 9.57 m2, entirely inside the margin strip, and it now has its greatest area on lot 3 and reaches that lot's buildable inset — so lot 3 carries a roof and lot 1 is what this parcel leaves open. THE CRITERION THAT NAMED LOT 3 IS KEPT HERE BECAUSE IT IS WHY LOT 3 WAS NAMED, not because it still has a choice to make: the Randolph frontage lot next to the Market corner was the farthest of this block's six free lots from the Dearborn Street drawbridge at 618.6 m, which is the test every block of the South Water row used to choose its open lot. Alternating vacancy is the programme's own assumption and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first block of the row ONE STREET BACK, and the first block of this parcel shape that is not on South Water Street: bounded by Lake, Franklin, Randolph and Market, at the western limit of the platted South Division against the south branch. Lots 0 and 1 arrive taken - the Lake-and-Market corner and the Randolph-and-Market corner - both seated by tools/plat_occupancy.py rather than authored here, so the schedule's six free lots are 2, 4 and 6 on Lake and 3, 5 and 7 on Randolph, and this parcel builds on five of them. THE FACE RULE IS INHERITED FROM FIVE BLOCKS OF SOUTH WATER STREET AND IS MEASURED HERE FOR THE FIRST TIME, BECAUSE NEITHER OF THIS BLOCK'S FACES IS SOUTH WATER. T-A8 through T-A12 sent their better dwellings to the business front and their meanest to the back street, and named the front by the street's documented use. That naming does not carry to a block whose two faces are Lake and Randolph, so the question was asked of the committed record instead: counting every documented or inferred structure whose footprint centroid stands within 25 m of a street's committed centreline, LAKE STREET CARRIES 12 AND RANDOLPH STREET CARRIES 2 - the Sauganash Hotel, the Green Tree Tavern, the Exchange Coffee House, the Tremont House, the Mansion House, both churches, Hogan's store, Goss & Cobb's saddlery, Pierce's blacksmith shop, Dole's south warehouse and Philo Carpenter's log drug store against the log jail and the Western Hotel. South Water itself carries 9. Lake is this block's better face by the town's own record, so the three best dwellings the schedule deals take its three free lots - the deep-plan cottage on lot 6, the two-room cottage on lot 4 and the one-room cottage on lot 2 - and the two meanest take Randolph, the plank shanty on lot 7 and the log cabin on lot 5. THE END RULE IS T-A11'S CRITERION, UNCHANGED, AND THIS BLOCK IS WHERE ITS MEANING THINS RATHER THAN ITS ORDER. Distance to the Dearborn Street drawbridge, the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835, runs 532.2 m at lot 6, 554.9 m at lot 4, 577.6 m at lot 2 and 600.4 m at lot 0 on the Lake frontage, with the back street from 576.3 m at lot 7 to 640.0 m at lot 1. The order is the same order the criterion has given on every block, and the arrangement follows it. What has changed is the size of the difference it is ordering: on T-A12's block the far end of the Lake frontage stood 2.93 times as far from the bridge as the near end, and on this one it stands 1.13 times as far. The whole spread of the front face is 68.2 m against T-A12's 70.2 m - the same block, moved half a kilometre - so the criterion is now separating two lots that are, in any terms a resident would have used, the same distance from the bridge. IT IS FOLLOWED ANYWAY AND THE REASON IS RECORDED RATHER THAN THE RESULT DEFENDED: a committed criterion applied where it is weak is re-derivable, and swapping to a second criterion on the block where the first one stops flattering the answer is how an invention starts looking like a finding. What it is NOT is evidence: no source says a better house stood nearer the bridge, and at this distance the arrangement is closer to arbitrary than it has been on any block of the row. LOT 3 IS LEFT OPEN AND IT IS THE FARTHEST FREE LOT FROM THE BRIDGE, at 618.6 m, which is the same test every block of the row has used. THE MEASUREMENT THIS BLOCK OWES ITS READER IS ROADMAP K30'S, AND IT IS THE FIRST ONE TAKEN OFF SOUTH WATER STREET. K30 records five documented buildings standing 4.5 m to 8.2 m inside the platted South Water corridor and asks whether that is a fault of one stretch of street or a uniform bias across the grid. This block carries the first two documented roofs measured against a different street: the SAUGANASH HOTEL intrudes 0.19 m into the Lake corridor and PHILO CARPENTER'S LOG DRUG STORE 0.22 m - a twentieth to a fortieth of the South Water figures, and within the plat's own precision of standing exactly on the kerb line. Two cases are not a survey, but they are the control measurement K30 did not have, and they point away from a uniform grid bias. Nothing here moves a documented position. THE BLOCK'S TWO DOCUMENTED ROOFS SHARE ONE LOT, AND THE MAP NAMES THE SMALLER OF THEM. The Sauganash Hotel puts 94.33 m2 of its 96.0 m2 on lot 0 (67.66 m2 inside the buildable inset) and Philo Carpenter's log drug store 28.58 m2 of its 29.7 m2 (19.43 m2 inside it); the source says the shop stood immediately east of and against the Sauganash's public bar and the two footprints touch at 0.00 m, so this is the record agreeing with itself rather than a collision. tools/plat_occupancy names the first holder by id, which is the log shop - the town's most-documented building is not the one the occupancy map credits with its own corner. It costs this parcel nothing, because the lot is taken either way, and the map's job is to say a lot is taken by something nameable. T-A7'S LAP CASE HAS A SIXTH INSTANCE AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT COSTS NOTHING TWICE: the packer's dwelling on lot 1 laps lot 3 by 9.57 m2 with 0.00 m2 of it inside lot 3's buildable inset, and lot 3 is the lot this parcel leaves open. The stable stands in the yard of lot 6 off the block alley, behind the deep-plan cottage on the Lake frontage - the best roof this parcel raises and the household of it that a horse is least implausible for - and the privy in the yard of lot 5 behind the log cabin on Randolph. Both stand on lots whose roofs this parcel also raised, which is what a yard building is a claim about.

refamilied.why: T-1682, piece 3 of 4 of T-1201, and it re-families ONE slot this block already built rather than dealing it any new ground. THE GROUND IS THE FINDING, and it is the same one T-1647 reached on the South Water row. T-1201 asked for the Lake frontage of the Franklin, La Salle, Wells, Market and Clinton blocks to stand as stores, and there is nowhere left to raise one: every one of the seven Lake-Randolph blocks reads `at_capacity` with headroom 0 in the 665-roof programme (clinton 11 standing of 31 capacity, market 10, franklin 14, wells 14, lasalle 14, clark 16, dearborn 13), so what the Lake business front is MADE OF can only change by saying what the roofs already standing on it are. AND ONLY TWO OF THE FIVE BLOCKS HOLD A ROOF THIS PROGRAMME MAY SPEAK FOR. blk_lake_wells, blk_lake_lasalle and blk_lake_clinton carry no record this parcel authored at all - their 14, 14 and 11 standing roofs belong to the research layer and to the phase-one South parcel, and a documented building is not this programme's to re-family. That is a refusal on the committed tree and not an omission: those three blocks' Lake frontage cannot be composed by this ticket in either direction. THE CARD THAT ASKS FOR IT: seq 01, the deep-plan frame cottage on lot 6's Lake frontage, is '[boot, shoe and leather store, Lake street, proprietor not recovered] - boot and shoe manufacturing and leather dealing', seated here by the street-face adoption policy off the Chicago Democrat. The source calls it a STORE in as many words and this programme had it standing as a cottage. WHAT IS LEFT AS IT STANDS, AND WHY: seq 02 and seq 03, the two-room and one-room frame cottages on lots 4 and 2, carry no `occupants` block at all - no trade asks either of them to be a store, and re-familying a roof the business layer says nothing about would be inventing the trade to justify the silhouette. Both keep their cottages. Seq 04 and seq 05 front randolph and are not on this ticket's ground. THE FAMILY IS THE EVIDENCE'S CHOICE AND THE CEILING IS MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED. C2, the store-residence, is the family a trade that MANUFACTURES AND DEALS belongs to - its own crosswalk variants read 'shop below; attic rooms; rear lean-to; signboard' - and that is what this card says the keeper does. C3 and C4 are two-storey stores and nothing on this card is evidence of a second storey or of the capital one implies; dealing one to make the frontage read richer is the confidence upgrade AGENTS.md rule 2 forbids, so the store-residence is the largest store family the EVIDENCE admits here rather than the largest the metres would take. C2's 18x30-22x40 ft band overlaps D5's 18x28-24x34, so the roof does not grow past the ground its slot already stood on. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE: the slot keeps its lot, setback, anchor and lateral offset, it is not promoted (it stays a `reconstructed` anonymous count-unit at the bottom tier), no occupant is invented - it keeps the one the street-face adoption policy already gave it - and the block is dealt no extra roof. The footprint is not authored here either: `generate_block_infill` samples a slot inside its family's own band on a stable key, so the record re-derives. THE ONE THING THAT DOES MOVE, AND THE RULE THAT MOVES IT: this slot stood 7.0 m back at a dwelling's typology setback, and `generate_block_infill.check_non_dwelling_slot` refuses a C roof there - 'a commercial roof stands ON the street line, at the 1.5 m the plat module's margin allows (T-0024)', because thirteen of the fourteen documented stores in this town do and a store's claim on frontage is functional. So the roof comes forward 5.5 m onto the same 1.5 m line every party-line run in this town already stands on. That is the policy's choice and not this ticket's: the refusal is quoted above, it was hit before anything was written, and the lot, the lateral offset and the face are unchanged.

open_lots.why: The Washington frontage lot at the Franklin corner, and the farthest of this block's seven free lots from the Dearborn Street drawbridge at 621.0 m, which is the test every block since T-A11 has used to choose its open lot. Alternating vacancy is the programme's own assumption and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target; which lot within the tier is still a choice, and this is the criterion that made it.

blocks.arrangement_note: The first block of the row TWO STREETS BACK, and the first block of this parcel shape NEITHER OF WHOSE FACES THE TOWN'S OWN RECORD CALLS A FRONT: bounded by Randolph, Wells, Washington and Franklin, one row south of the Randolph frontage the row before it built. Lot 2 arrives taken - Harmon's log cabin on the Randolph face - seated by tools/plat_occupancy.py rather than authored here, so the schedule's seven free lots are 0, 4 and 6 on Randolph and 1, 3, 5 and 7 on Washington, and this parcel builds on six of them. THE FACE RULE IS MEASURED AGAIN, BECAUSE T-A13 MEASURED THE WRONG PAIR FOR THIS BLOCK AND ITS FIGURES DO NOT REPRODUCE. T-A13 chose between Lake and Randolph by counting structures within 25 m of each street's committed centreline and reported Lake 12, Randolph 2, South Water 9; those three numbers cannot be recovered from the committed record under the filter its note states, and the filter it actually used is not written down anywhere. The measurement is therefore re-derived here by a committed tool - tools/measure_street_frontage.py - so that the next block inherits a command rather than a remembered number. Counting every structure record whose footprint centroid stands within 25 m of a street's committed centreline, reported by layer because the three are not the same kind of evidence: RANDOLPH carries 7 research-layer records (Newberry & Dole's south-branch slaughterhouse, the log jail, the Cook County courthouse, both Wright buildings to let, Harmon's log cabin and the Western Hotel) and 7 inferred-household buildings; WASHINGTON carries 1 research-layer record - the estray pen, the town's pound for stray animals - and no inferred-household building at all. That is 14 against 1. The third layer is the anonymous count-units the block parcels themselves place, and it is excluded rather than merged, because a block parcel that let it vote would be reading its own output back as evidence: it stood at 15 on Randolph and 9 on Washington when this choice was made and reads 18 and 12 after this parcel built, which is the whole demonstration. Re-measured by the same tool on the same day, Lake carries 17 research-layer records and South Water 14, so T-A13's Lake 12 / Randolph 2 / South Water 9 was not this filter. Randolph is this block's better face by the same test T-A13 named, by a margin no reading of the filter changes, and the whole of Washington Street's documented 1835 frontage is a pen for stray animals. It is still the invention it has always been: no source says a better dwelling stood on the better street. SO THE THREE BEST DWELLINGS THE SCHEDULE DEALS TAKE RANDOLPH'S THREE FREE LOTS - the one-and-a-half-storey cottage on lot 6, the deep-plan cottage on lot 4 and the two-room cottage on lot 0 - and the three meanest take Washington: the one-room cottage on lot 7, the plank shanty on lot 5 and the log cabin on lot 3. THE END RULE IS T-A11'S CRITERION, UNCHANGED, AND ITS SPREAD HAS THINNED AGAIN. Distance to the Dearborn Street drawbridge, the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835, runs 527.8 m at lot 6, 546.1 m at lot 4 and 584.0 m at lot 0 on the Randolph frontage, with the back street from 568.5 m at lot 7 to 621.0 m at lot 1. The order is the order the criterion has given on every block. The far end of the front face stands 1.11 times as far from the bridge as the near end, against T-A13's 1.13 and T-A12's 2.93, and the absolute spread of the front face is 56.2 m against T-A13's 68.2 m - so this block is the second in a row on which the criterion separates lots that a resident would have called the same distance from the bridge, and the arrangement it produces is closer to arbitrary than ordered. It is followed anyway, for T-A13's reason: swapping criteria on the block where the first stops flattering the answer is how an invention starts to look like a finding. THE YARD BUILDINGS STAND BEHIND THE BEST ROOF AND THE MEANEST, as T-A13's did: the stable in the alley yard of lot 6 behind the one-and-a-half-storey cottage, the privy in the alley yard of lot 3 behind the log cabin.

open_lots.why: The Washington frontage lot at the Clark corner, and the farthest of this block's seven free lots from the Dearborn Street drawbridge at 388.2 m, which is the test every block since T-A11 has used to choose its open lot. Alternating vacancy is the programme's own assumption and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target; which lot within the tier is still a choice, and this is the criterion that made it. The criterion is weaker here than it has ever been - 388.2 m against 376.4 m at the near end of the same face, a spread of 11.8 m across four lots - so read the arrangement note's end-rule paragraph and ROADMAP K31 before leaning on it on the next block of this row.

blocks.arrangement_note: THE BLOCK BETWEEN THE COURTHOUSE AND THE BRIDGE. Bounded by Randolph, Dearborn, Washington and Clark, on the same row two streets back from the business front that T-A14 opened, but at the other end of it: its west face stands across Clark Street from the public square block (blk_randolph_lasalle, which carries the Cook County courthouse, both Wright buildings to let and the estray pen), and its east face IS Dearborn Street, the street of the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835. One roof arrives standing - the gunsmith's shop on lot 0, an inferred-household building on the Randolph face, seated by tools/plat_occupancy.py rather than authored here - so the schedule's seven free lots are 2, 4 and 6 on Randolph and 1, 3, 5 and 7 on Washington, and this parcel builds on six of them. THE SCHEDULE DEALT THIS BLOCK THE TOWN'S BETTER HOUSES, AND THAT IS A COINCIDENCE RATHER THAN A FINDING. The eight roofs are H2 (merchant or professional house), H1 (larger one-and-a-half-storey house), C2 (store-residence), D6, D2, D1 and the two yard buildings A4 and A3 - the first time a platted block parcel has been dealt both H families together, and the first C2 any block parcel has stood, though four C2 roofs already stand elsewhere in the town and blk_randolph_wells built an H1 and an H2 at T-A2. It is tempting to read the deal as the schedule recognising the block opposite the courthouse. It is not: the apportionment is a district remainder spread across schedule units by tools/reconcile_665.py and is BLIND to what stands across the street. The agreement between the deal and the situation is recorded here so that no later parcel mistakes it for evidence. THE FACE RULE IS MEASURED, NOT REMEMBERED, per T-A14. tools/measure_street_frontage.py randolph washington, counting every structure record whose footprint centroid stands within 25 m of the street's committed centreline and reporting the three evidence layers separately: RANDOLPH carries 7 research-layer records (Newberry & Dole's south-branch slaughterhouse, the log jail, the Cook County courthouse, both Wright buildings to let, Harmon's log cabin and the Western Hotel) and 7 inferred-household buildings; WASHINGTON carries 1 research-layer record - the estray pen, the town's pound for stray animals - and no inferred-household building at all. That is 14 against 1, the same margin T-A14 measured on the same pair of streets, and it reproduces exactly. The third layer is the anonymous count-units the block parcels themselves place; it read 18 on Randolph and 12 on Washington when this arrangement was chosen and is excluded rather than merged, because a block parcel that let it vote would be reading its own output back as evidence. Randolph is this block's better face. It is still the invention it has always been: no source says a better dwelling stood on the better street. SO RANDOLPH'S THREE FREE LOTS TAKE THE STORE AND THE TWO BEST HOUSES - and the third of those three is a rule this parcel EXTENDED rather than applied. The face rule as committed at T-A13 and T-A14 ranks DWELLINGS: the best dwellings take the better street and the meanest take the back one. It says nothing about a store, and this is the first block that has had to place one. The extension made here is that a store-residence's claim on the better frontage is functional rather than social - it is the only one of the six roofs whose purpose requires that a stranger can find it, and the whole documented frontage of the alternative is a pen for stray animals. So C2 takes Randolph and the one-and-a-half-storey cottage D6, which would have taken the third front lot under the rule as written, goes to the back street at the head of its face. The extension is flagged as ROADMAP K32: the next block dealt a commercial family should follow it or refute it, not re-decide it privately. THE END RULE IS EXHAUSTED ON THIS BLOCK, AND THIS PARCEL MEASURED WHY. Distance to the Dearborn Street drawbridge runs 318.3 m at lot 6, 321.1 m at lot 4 and 325.8 m at lot 2 on the Randolph frontage, and 376.4 m at lot 7, 378.8 m at lot 5, 382.7 m at lot 3 and 388.2 m at lot 1 behind. The far end of the front face stands 1.02 times as far from the bridge as the near end, against T-A14's 1.11, T-A13's 1.13 and T-A12's 2.93, and the front face's absolute spread is 7.5 m - less than a third of one lot's 24.6 m frontage. The reason is geometric and not particular to this block: the bridge bears 10.4 degrees east of north from the block centre while the block face runs east-west, so the criterion can only see sin(10.4 deg) = 18 per cent of any displacement along the street. The 49.3 m between the lot 2 and lot 6 centroids projects to 8.9 m of range, and 7.5 m is what survives. A criterion that separates three lots by 7.5 m is not ordering them; it is breaking a tie with rounding. It is followed anyway, for T-A13's reason - swapping criteria on the block where the first stops flattering the answer is how an invention starts to look like a finding - and the successor question is opened as ROADMAP K31 rather than answered here. Note that on THIS block the committed rule and a stronger one agree: lot 6 is the block's corner on Dearborn Street, the street that carries the bridge, so the same lot wins under distance-as-measured and under frontage-on-the-bridge-street. That agreement is why following the exhausted rule costs nothing here, and it is exactly what K31 must not assume holds on the next block. THE BACK STREET TAKES THE THREE MEANEST, in the same order: the one-and-a-half-storey cottage on lot 7, the plank shanty D2 on lot 5 and the older log cabin D1 on lot 3, with lot 1 - the farthest free lot from the bridge - left open. THE YARD BUILDINGS STAND BEHIND THE BEST ROOF AND THE MEANEST, as T-A13 and T-A14 both did: the woodshed A4 in the alley yard of lot 6 behind the store-residence, because a store keeps stock and fuel and is the roof on this block most likely to need a dry shed, and the privy A3 in the alley yard of lot 3 behind the log cabin. Every setback and lateral offset below is a period typology bounded by the lot, not a measurement of it, and no lot is numbered: this project has never read Thompson's numbering off a sheet. THE EXTENSION THIS PARCEL FLAGGED AS K32 IS SETTLED, AND THE STORE COMES FORWARD (T-0024). The ranking above is REFUSED as a rule: the face rule ranks dwellings, and a non-dwelling is placed by its function, read off the documented record rather than reasoned about — see this file's placement_rule.non_dwelling_placement. On this block the two readings agree, so the C2 keeps Randolph and the D6 keeps the head of Washington: nothing is re-dealt and no household moves. What changes is the SETBACK, which is what the word 'functional' in the extension's own sentence actually buys. This parcel had stood the store 4.5 m back, the shallowest of the three Randolph roofs but still inside the 4.0–7.5 m typology band the block deals its dwellings — so a building whose whole argument was that a stranger must be able to find it stood in the line of house fronts. Every documented store in this town that stands on a platted street stands on its line. The C2 now does too, at 1.50 m, the closest line the plat module's own margin allows and the same line the party-line runs on South Water and Lake already stand on. It is the only roof on the block that moves, it moves 3.0 m, and it keeps its id, family, footprint, form values, lot and lateral offset.

drawn_from_gated_ground.why: THE SCHEDULE OWES THE SOUTH DIVISION FOUR WORKSHOPS AND HOLDS ALL FOUR WHERE NOTHING CAN STAND. The 665-roof schedule (data/reconstruction/1835_665_roof_programme.json) deals the South's last workshops onto two gated units: a blacksmith's shop (W1) and a carpenter's shop (W2) on blk_south_water_market, which is gated, and two carpenter's shops (W2) on south_plat_beyond_committed_control, the district balance that waits on survey control nobody has read. The order book's structures/workshops/south row reads 15 targeted, 11 standing, 4 to build. Every block of the original town with a face a workshop may take reads at_capacity, because its headroom is counted a free lot to a principal roof and a rear shop takes no lot. So these shops are drawn from the gated ground by family, one for one, and the schedule re-derives with them standing: the gated units' workshop count falls by what stands here, and no family total moves.

open_lots.why: The lot the first deal on this block named open, still open. The schedule keeps one free lot open on every block, and two rear shops on lots already built on take no lot of their own.

blocks.arrangement_note: A SHOP AT THE BACK OF THE CORNER LOT, ITS DOOR ON DEARBORN STREET (T-2134). The house already standing on this corner lot fronts the block's long face; the shop stands at the other end of the same lot, behind it, 1.55 m back from the Dearborn Street line — on the street line, where the placement policy's `mechanics_streets` clause puts a shop and where the town's boarding houses already stand — and 14 m along it from the middle of the lot's side toward the block alley, with its gable to the street. It is ancillary by position under the owner's ruling of 2026-09-23 that a lot may carry a main house plus a rear building (reconcile_665.inventory_class reads it so), so it adds no house to the frontage and the lot ceiling counts the lot exactly as before. DEARBORN IS THE FACE A SHOP MAY TAKE HERE: it is `ordinary` in data/streets/1835.json, no face of this block outranks it, and five of the town's seven documented workshops stand on an ordinary street. WHAT IS INVENTED IS EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a shop stood on this lot in 1835, which trade it served, where on the lot it stood and how far back. No source places a workshop here; the shop is an anonymous count-unit at the bottom tier, recorded in docs/LIBERTIES.md (L389).

open_lots.why: The Randolph frontage lot east of the Clark corner, and the farther of this block's two free lots from the Dearborn Street drawbridge at 215.8 m against lot 0's 177.9 m — the test every block of this row has used to choose its open lot since T-A11 replaced a compass direction with a measured one. It is also on the block's BACK face by the same block's own criterion: counting every committed structure that is not an anonymous count-unit and whose position stands within 25 m of a street's committed centreline, Lake Street carries 21 and Randolph Street 13 — 15 against 6 if only the documented records are counted. Alternating vacancy is the programme's own assumption and the schedule's capacity is a ceiling rather than a target; which lot within the tier is still a choice, and this is the criterion that made it.

frontage.adopts_face_line_why: T-0104. THIS FACE WAS ALREADY BUILT WHEN THIS RUN ARRIVED, and it was built to a different line. T-0077 stood four anonymous roofs on this same Lake frontage with their front walls 0.80 m off it; this run stood three more 1.50 m off it, because 1.50 m is the plat module's own lot margin and no rule had ever asked what the face was already carrying. Ten metres of open frontage between the two runs is the only reason the face did not read as a step, and the next parcel to close that gap would have put a 0.70 m jog in a street wall this project describes everywhere as one line. Measured, the face carried worse than two lines: inf_bakery_lake and inf_butcher_market, the two inferred-household buildings T-0077 aligned ITS row to, stand at 0.804 m and 0.784 m at bearing 0 where this face runs at 0.465 - so they are not on any line at all, and the 0.80 m T-0077 adopted was a reading of them rather than a rule. Of the three routes T-0104 set out this is (b): the run stands closer than the lot margin on the STREET line specifically. It is taken because (a) - moving T-0077's row out to 1.50 m - would have broken the party wall recon_1835_south_d3_013 declares with inf_butcher_market and CREATED the jog the ticket exists to prevent, on the one wall in the row that is gated as a shared wall. The exemption is as narrow as L141's: it reaches the street line only, the side lot lines keep the full 1.50 m margin, and the number is not authored here - `adopts_face_line` names the committed records and tools/generate_block_infill.py measures their front walls, so a recipe that states any other setback fails. What no line here claims is a measurement of 1835: both numbers are inventions, and the only thing being chosen is that the face carries one of them.
frontage.why: T-0079, the third and last piece of the owner's flagged-important ask of 2026-08-18: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." THIS RUN IS THE DEMONSTRATION OF THE CORE DENSITY STANDARD and it is the first row in this project to stand three roofs on one lot. The old gate made a run carry exactly one roof per lot it was dealt, so this block's single free Lake lot could take a single cottage set back in the middle of it — which is the shape the owner's Tremont Street reference (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md, image 5) is a picture of the town NOT having. The standard's ceiling is three units per lot, measured at the smallest lot on the committed grid, and this run spends all three. IT BUILDS TO THE CORNER, which is the clause of the standard no run could satisfy before it: anchored on the WEST end of its own frontage, the log dwelling's west wall stands 1.5 m from the Clark side line — the closest line the plat module's own margin allows — and the other two chain east off its wall in turn. WITHIN THE RUN THE END RULE ORDERS THEM, unchanged from every block of this row: better roofs nearer the town-centre end, which here is east toward Dearborn and the only crossing of the main stem in July 1835. So the log dwelling takes the Clark corner, the one-room cottage stands next to it and the deep-plan cottage closes the run at the east end, 10.58 m short of the bakery that already stands on the next lot. THIS RUN EXTENDS T-0077'S ROW ON THE SAME FACE: recon_1835_south_d3_013, inf_butcher_market, recon_1835_south_d4_014, recon_1835_south_d5_016 and recon_1835_south_c3_015 already stand shoulder to shoulder from 63.56 m to 97.57 m along this face, and inf_bakery_lake at 28.93 m to 34.49 m; the new run occupies 1.50 m to 18.36 m, so the Lake face of this block now carries built frontage at its west corner, its middle and its east end. NO COORDINATE IS AUTHORED HERE: the line, its bearing and the end the run packs away from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and the 1.5 m setback is the plat module's own lot margin rather than a measurement of this frontage.
